assignment.title: Rational Exponents — Honors
assignment.essentialQuestion: Why can it be useful to simplify expressions?
assignment.teacherNotes: Honors version of Bluebonnet Algebra II — Radicals, Lesson 3 (Rational Exponents), TEKS A2.7G. Beyond the regular lesson: exponent rules on monomials with rational and negative exponents, combining radicals with different indices, roots of roots, factoring out rational powers, comparing powers without a calculator, why (−8)^(4/6) misleads, products that reverse the factoring patterns, and power models (Kepler’s third law, surface-area scaling, Kleiber’s law). Answers are graded in the notation the key uses (a radical-form key needs a radical; an exponential-form key a rational exponent), in simplest form, and exact where asked. Practice includes two audited SAT items (MathMaster CCMR bank). Warm-Up and DOL are generated per student and back Recovery.

questions.prompt: Evaluate exactly: ${{b}}^{-\frac{ {{m}} }{ {{n}} }}$. Show the root first.
hints: A negative exponent means the reciprocal.
Take the root first, then the power.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. b^(−r) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Reciprocal, root, power.
reasoning: Raise {{c}} to the power {{m}}: {{v}}. So the value is 1/{{v}}.
solutionReview.commonError: Making the answer negative: a negative exponent gives a reciprocal, not a negative number.

questions.prompt: Write $\sqrt[{{n}}]{x^{ {{m}} }}$ as a power of $x$ with the exponent in lowest terms. Assume $x > 0$.
hints: The index of the root is the denominator of the exponent.
Reduce the fraction.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In x^(m/n), the denominator n is…

solutionReview.headline: Root index → denominator, power → numerator; then reduce.
reasoning: The index-{{n}} root of x^{{m}} is x^({{m}}/{{n}}).
solutionReview.commonError: Leaving x^({{m}}/{{n}}): the exponent is not in lowest terms.

questions.prompt: Simplify with positive exponents: $\left(x^{ {{e}} }\right)^{-\frac{ {{m}} }{ {{n}} }}$
hints: Power of a power: multiply the exponents.
A negative exponent means the reciprocal.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (x^a)^b equals…

solutionReview.headline: Multiply the exponents, then take the reciprocal.
solutionReview.commonError: Adding the exponents instead of multiplying them: a power of a power multiplies, then the negative exponent moves x to the denominator.

questions.prompt: The exponent rules hold for rational exponents. Simplify with positive exponents only: $\left(27x^{-6}y^9\right)^{\frac{2}{3}}$ and $\left(16a^8b^{-4}\right)^{-\frac{3}{4}}$.

steps.title: The same rules
steps.instruction: For rational exponents: a^r · a^s = a^(r+s), a^r / a^s = a^(r−s), (a^r)^s = a^(rs), (ab)^r = a^r b^r, a^(−r) = 1/a^r.

steps.title: Simplified form
steps.instruction: Positive exponents, each base once, exponents in lowest terms, no fractional exponent in a denominator.

hints: Raise each factor to the outside power: (abc)^r = a^r b^r c^r.
For the numbers, take the root first: 27^(1/3) and 16^(1/4).

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (x⁻⁶)^(2/3) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Raise each factor to the power, then clear negative exponents.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying 27 by 2/3: a rational exponent on a number means a root and a power, not multiplication.

questions.prompt: Different indices. Rational exponents let you combine radicals with different indices. Simplify $\sqrt{2} \cdot \sqrt[3]{2}$ and $\sqrt[4]{x^3} \cdot \sqrt[3]{x}$.

steps.title: Different indices
steps.instruction: Rewrite each radical with a rational exponent, use the exponent rules, then convert back. Example: √x · ∛x = x^(1/2 + 1/3) = x^(5/6) = ⁶√(x⁵).

steps.title: Exponents greater than 1
steps.instruction: x^(7/4) = x^(4/4) · x^(3/4) = x ∜(x³): a whole power comes out of the radical.

hints: Add the exponents with a common denominator.
An exponent greater than 1 splits into a whole number plus a fraction less than 1.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. ∛2 written with a rational exponent is…

solutionReview.headline: Exponents first, radicals last.
solutionReview.commonError: Multiplying the radicands under a mixed index: √2 · ∛2 is not ⁵√4 or ⁶√4.

questions.prompt: Quotients and roots of roots. Simplify $\dfrac{\sqrt{x}}{\sqrt[3]{x}}$ and $\sqrt{\sqrt[3]{x}}$, and evaluate $\sqrt[3]{\sqrt{64}}$. Assume $x > 0$.

responses.label: Why do √(∛x) and ∛(√x) give the same result?
options: Both are x^((1/2)(1/3)) = x^(1/6), and the order of multiplication does not matter
They do not: one of them is x^(1/5)
Because square roots and cube roots are the same
responses.answer: Both are x^((1/2)(1/3)) = x^(1/6), and the order of multiplication does not matter

hints: Divide powers with the same base by subtracting exponents.
A root of a root multiplies the exponents.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (x^a)^b equals…

solutionReview.headline: Subtract exponents to divide; multiply them for a root of a root.
solutionReview.commonError: Dividing the exponents instead of subtracting them: √x / ∛x is x^(1/2 − 1/3), not x^(3/2).

questions.prompt: Factoring with rational exponents. The GCF uses the smallest exponent, even when it is a fraction or negative. Factor $x^{\frac{3}{2}} - x^{\frac{1}{2}}$, $\;2x^{\frac{5}{3}} + 6x^{\frac{2}{3}}$ and $\;x^{\frac{1}{2}} + x^{-\frac{1}{2}}$.

steps.title: Factoring with rational exponents
steps.instruction: Take out the smallest power of each base, then divide each term by it (subtract exponents). Example: x^(5/2) + 3x^(3/2) = x^(3/2)(x + 3).

hints: Take out the smallest power of x, together with the GCF of the coefficients.
Divide each term by the GCF: subtract exponents.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. x^(3/2) ÷ x^(1/2) equals…

solutionReview.headline: Smallest exponent out; subtract exponents for what is left.
reasoning: The smaller exponent is 1/2: x^(3/2) ÷ x^(1/2) = x and x^(1/2) ÷ x^(1/2) = 1, so x^(1/2)(x − 1).
solutionReview.commonError: Taking out the larger exponent: x^(3/2)(1 − x^(−1)) leaves a negative exponent inside.

questions.prompt: Compare without a calculator. Raise both numbers to a power that clears the fractions, then compare: (a) $2^{\frac{1}{2}}$ and $3^{\frac{1}{3}}$; (b) $\sqrt{5}$ and $\sqrt[3]{11}$.

responses.label: (a) Which is larger?
options: It cannot be decided without a calculator

responses.label: (b) Which is larger?
options: It cannot be decided without a calculator

hints: One power clears both 1/2 and 1/3.
For positive numbers, raising both to the same positive power keeps their order.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Which power clears the exponents 1/2 and 1/3 at once?

solutionReview.headline: Same power on both sides keeps the order.
solutionReview.commonError: Comparing the exponents alone: with different bases, compare the numbers raised to a power that clears the fractions.

questions.prompt: Error analysis. Three students evaluate $(-8)^{\frac{2}{3}}$. Pat: $\left((-8)^2\right)^{\frac{1}{3}} = 64^{\frac{1}{3}} = 4$. Sam: $\left(\sqrt[3]{-8}\right)^2 = (-2)^2 = 4$. Lee: $(-8)^{\frac{2}{3}} = (-8)^{\frac{4}{6}} = \left(\sqrt[6]{-8}\right)^4$, which is not a real number.

responses.label: Why?
options: Rewriting 2/3 as 4/6 brings in an even root of a negative number, which is not real; with a negative base, keep the exponent in lowest terms
The cube root of a negative number is not real
A negative base can never have a rational exponent
responses.answer: Rewriting 2/3 as 4/6 brings in an even root of a negative number, which is not real; with a negative base, keep the exponent in lowest terms

hints: Check each step: which one takes an even root of a negative number?
The cube root of −8 is a real number.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Is ∛(−8) a real number?

solutionReview.headline: Equivalent exponents are not always equivalent for a negative base.
reasoning: Pat and Sam both get 4: (−8)² = 64 and ∛64 = 4; ∛(−8) = −2 and (−2)² = 4.
Lee rewrote 2/3 as 4/6. ⁶√(−8) is an even root of a negative number, so it is not real.
b^(m/n) = (ⁿ√b)^m needs ⁿ√b to be real, so for a negative base keep the exponent in lowest terms.
solutionReview.commonError: Rewriting the exponent of a negative base: (−8)^(4/6) brings in an even root of a negative number, so keep 2/3 in lowest terms.

questions.prompt: Products with rational exponents. Multiply and simplify $\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}} + y^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}} - y^{\frac{1}{2}}\right)$ and $\left(x^{\frac{1}{3}} + 2\right)\left(x^{\frac{2}{3}} - 2x^{\frac{1}{3}} + 4\right)$.

responses.label: The second product is an example of…
options: the sum of cubes, a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²), with a = x^(1/3) and b = 2
no pattern: the terms just happen to cancel
responses.answer: the sum of cubes, a³ + b³ = (a + b)(a² − ab + b²), with a = x^(1/3) and b = 2

hints: The first is (a + b)(a − b) = a² − b².
Multiply the second term by term, or recognize a pattern from the factoring lesson.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (x^(1/2))² equals…

solutionReview.headline: Factoring patterns run backwards.
reasoning: With a = x^(1/3) and b = 2: (a + b)(a² − ab + b²) = a³ + b³ = (x^(1/3))³ + 2³ = x + 8.
solutionReview.commonError: Squaring x^(1/2) as x^(1/4): a power of a power multiplies the exponents, so (x^(1/2))² = x.

responses.label: In simplest radical form, T = a^(3/2) =
A planet with a period of 8 years: a = 8^(2/3) =
An asteroid at a = 9 AU: T = 9^(3/2) =
Mars (table): T ≈ (years, to the nearest hundredth)

hints: For b^(2/3), take the cube root first, then square.
For b^(3/2), take the square root first, then cube.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. In b^(3/2), which root do you take first?

solutionReview.headline: Root first keeps the numbers small.
reasoning: 5.20^(3/2) = 5.20 · √5.20 ≈ 5.20 · 2.280 ≈ 11.9, which matches Jupiter’s 11.86 years in the table.
solutionReview.answerSummary: a√a; 4 AU; 27 years; about 1.87 years; about 11.9, matching the table
solutionReview.commonError: Evaluating 8^(2/3) as 8²/3 or (8/3)²: take the cube root first, then square.

questions.prompt: Modeling: scaling. For similar solids, surface area grows like volume to the $\tfrac{2}{3}$ power: if the volume is multiplied by $k$, the surface area is multiplied by $k^{\frac{2}{3}}$. (This is one reason a large animal loses heat more slowly, pound for pound, than a small one.)

responses.label: The volume is multiplied by 8. The surface area is multiplied by
The volume is multiplied by 27. The surface area is multiplied by
The surface area is multiplied by 16. The volume is multiplied by

hints: Multiplying the volume by k multiplies the surface area by k^(2/3).
To undo the power 2/3, raise both sides to the power 3/2.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. What power undoes the power 2/3?

solutionReview.headline: Rational powers model scaling.
solutionReview.commonError: Swapping the powers: the area factor is (volume factor)^(2/3), so a volume factor of 8 gives 4, not 8^(3/2).

questions.prompt: Same power, different forms. Assume x > 0. Sort each expression by the single power of x it equals.
hints: Rewrite each expression with a single rational exponent.
Reduce each exponent to lowest terms.

solutionReview.headline: Write each card as one power of x, then reduce the exponent.
solutionReview.commonError: ∛(x²) is x^(2/3), not x^(3/2): the power goes on top and the index on the bottom.

hints: Rewrite each radical with a rational exponent.
Add the exponents with a common denominator.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. The index-n root of x^a, written as a power of x, is…

solutionReview.headline: Rational exponents, then a common denominator.
reasoning: The index-{{n}} root of x^{{a}} is x^({{a}}/{{n}}), and the index-{{m}} root of x^{{b}} is x^({{b}}/{{m}}).
solutionReview.commonError: Adding the fractions straight across: exponents like a/n + b/m need a common denominator.

hints: Take out the smallest power of x, together with the GCF of the coefficients.
Divide each term by the GCF: subtract exponents.

solutionReview.headline: Smallest exponent out; subtract exponents for what is left.

questions.prompt: Evaluate exactly: $\left(-{{cn}}\right)^{\frac{ {{m}} }{ {{n}} }}$. Show the root first.
hints: An odd root of a negative number is negative.
Take the root first, then raise it to the power.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Is ∛(−8) a real number?

solutionReview.headline: An odd root keeps the sign.
reasoning: Raise −{{c}} to the power {{m}}: the value is {{v}}.
solutionReview.commonError: Thinking a negative base makes the answer not real: an odd root of a negative number is real, and negative.

hints: Raise all three to one power that clears every denominator.
Raising positive numbers to the same positive power keeps their order.

solutionReview.headline: Compare sixth powers.
solutionReview.commonError: Ordering by the exponents or the bases alone: compare the sixth powers, 8, 9 and 6.

questions.prompt: Error analysis. A classmate writes $(x + 9)^{\frac{1}{2}} = x^{\frac{1}{2}} + 3$ and $(x^2)^{\frac{1}{2}} = x$ for every real $x$. Test each claim.

responses.label: So (x + 9)^(1/2) = x^(1/2) + 3 is…
options: false: an exponent does not distribute over a sum
true only when x is a perfect square
responses.answer: false: an exponent does not distribute over a sum

responses.label: For which x is (x²)^(1/2) = x?
options: x ≥ 0; for x < 0 it equals −x, so (x²)^(1/2) = |x|
responses.answer: x ≥ 0; for x < 0 it equals −x, so (x²)^(1/2) = |x|

hints: Substitute x = 16 into both sides of the first claim.
Try x = −3 in (x²)^(1/2).

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. Does (a + b)^r equal a^r + b^r for every r?

solutionReview.headline: Test claims with numbers; one counterexample is enough.
reasoning: Exponents distribute over products, (ab)^r = a^r b^r, never over sums.
At x = −3: ((−3)²)^(1/2) = 9^(1/2) = 3, not −3. So (x²)^(1/2) = |x|, which equals x only when x ≥ 0.
solutionReview.commonError: Distributing an exponent over a sum: (x + 9)^(1/2) is not x^(1/2) + 3.

questions.prompt: Simplify with positive exponents only: $\dfrac{\left(x^{\frac{1}{2}}y^{-\frac{2}{3}}\right)^6}{\left(x^{-1}y^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)^3}$
hints: Power of a product: multiply each exponent by the outside power.
Dividing powers of the same base subtracts the exponents.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (y^(−2/3))⁶ equals…

solutionReview.headline: Powers of products, then quotients of powers.
solutionReview.commonError: Dividing by x⁻³ the wrong way: subtracting a negative exponent adds 3 to the exponent of x.

questions.prompt: For $x>0$, what is the value of $\dfrac{\sqrt{{{a2}}x^5}}{\sqrt{x}}$ when $x={{xval}}$?

optionRationales.{{answer}}: {{a}}x^(5/2) ÷ x^(1/2) = {{a}}x², and at x = {{xval}} that is {{answer}}.
optionRationales.{{dDroppedCoefficient}}: {{dDroppedCoefficient}} is x² alone; √{{a2}} = {{a}} still multiplies it.
optionRationales.{{dRoundedUp}}: {{dRoundedUp}} keeps too high a power of x; subtract the exponents 5/2 − 1/2.
optionRationales.{{dSquaredCoefficient}}: {{dSquaredCoefficient}} keeps {{a2}} instead of its square root and uses x to the first power.

solutionReview.headline: Write the radicals as powers and subtract exponents.
solutionReview.commonError: Forgetting the coefficient: √{{a2}} = {{a}} still multiplies x².

questions.prompt: Factor $x - 27$ as a difference of cubes, using $x = \left(x^{\frac{1}{3}}\right)^3$.

responses.label: Why can x − 27 be factored this way?
options: x = (x^(1/3))³ and 27 = 3³, so x − 27 is a difference of cubes
x − 27 is a difference of squares
Every binomial is a difference of cubes
responses.answer: x = (x^(1/3))³ and 27 = 3³, so x − 27 is a difference of cubes

hints: a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²).
Here a = x^(1/3) and b = 3.

scaffold.prompt: Let’s back up. (x^(1/3))³ equals…

solutionReview.headline: A difference of cubes with a = x^(1/3).
solutionReview.commonError: Using − inside the trinomial: a³ − b³ = (a − b)(a² + ab + b²), and the trinomial’s signs are all +.

questions.prompt: Simplify with positive exponents: $\left({{cn}}x^{ {{nk}} }\right)^{-\frac{ {{m}} }{ {{n}} }}$

solutionReview.headline: Reciprocal, then raise each factor to the power.

questions.prompt: Write as a single power of $x$ in lowest terms: $\sqrt[{{n}}]{x^{ {{a}} }} \cdot \sqrt[{{m}}]{x^{ {{b}} }}$. Assume $x > 0$.

solutionReview.headline: Rational exponents, then a common denominator.
reasoning: The index-{{n}} root of x^{{a}} is x^({{a}}/{{n}}), and the index-{{m}} root of x^{{b}} is x^({{b}}/{{m}}).

questions.prompt: Factor out the greatest common factor: ${{g|coef}}x^{\frac{ {{aq}} }{ {{q}} }} {{gc|signed}}x^{\frac{ {{a}} }{ {{q}} }}$

solutionReview.headline: Smallest exponent out; subtract exponents for what is left.
reasoning: The smaller exponent is {{a}}/{{q}}, so the GCF is {{g|coef}}x^({{a}}/{{q}}).
solutionReview.commonError: Factoring out the larger power of x: the GCF takes the smaller exponent.
